question: What if the Bronze Age world had not collapsed around 1177 BCE?
short: Around 1200 to 1150 BCE the palace states of the eastern Mediterranean fell together: Mycenae and Pylos, the Hittites, Ugarit, while Egypt barely held. Drought, earthquakes, raiders and broken trade all hit at once. Take away the worst of the drought and the palaces may limp on, keeping their scribes, their bronze trade and their monopolies longer. The alphabet, iron and the small new states of the Iron Age might all have come later.

divergence.text: The long dry spell of about 1250 to 1100 BCE is milder, so the harvests hold.

plausibility_note: Low: the collapse had many causes, and removing one (drought) may not save a system already strained by war, raids and rigid palace economies.

steps.title: A world on one ship
steps.text: The Uluburun ship, sunk off southern Turkey around 1300 BCE, carried about ten tonnes of Cypriot copper, a tonne of tin, glass ingots, ebony, ivory and gold. Bronze needs both metals, which come from far apart, so the palaces depended on long-distance trade.

sources.cite: Eric Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014)

steps.title: The dry century
steps.text: Pollen cores from the Sea of Galilee and lake sediments in Cyprus and Syria point to a long dry phase from about 1250 to 1100 BCE. Letters from Ugarit and the Hittite court talk of grain shipments and famine. This is the lever the what-if pulls.

sources.cite: Dafna Langgut, Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Litt, Climate and the Late Bronze collapse, Tel Aviv 40 (2013)
David Kaniewski et al., Environmental roots of the Late Bronze Age crisis, PLOS ONE (2013)

steps.title: Ugarit's last letters
steps.text: Ugarit on the Syrian coast was destroyed around 1190-1185 BCE; tablets found in its ruins ask for help against enemy ships. The Hittite capital Hattusa was abandoned about the same time, and the Mycenaean palaces at Pylos and Mycenae burned.

steps.title: Egypt holds the Delta
steps.text: In his eighth year (about 1177 BCE) Ramesses III fought the 'Sea Peoples' by land and in the Delta, and carved the victory on his temple at Medinet Habu. Egypt survived, but smaller and poorer, and lost its empire in the Levant within a century.

steps.title: The palaces limp on
steps.text: With harvests holding, palace economies that taxed and redistributed grain keep their footing. Linear B scribes keep writing, and Greece skips or shortens the three-century 'Dark Age' in which writing vanished. But Cline's point is that the system broke because many things failed at once; drought relief alone may only buy time.

steps.title: The alphabet's big chance, delayed
steps.text: The Phoenician alphabet spread in the century after the collapse, when the big scribal bureaucracies were gone and small coastal cities traded on their own. Keep the palaces and their trained scribes, with their cuneiform and Linear B, and the cheap 22-letter script may spread more slowly. Speculative, but it follows the actors' interests.

steps.title: Iron comes later
steps.text: Anthony Snodgrass argued that broken tin routes pushed smiths toward local iron. If the bronze trade had survived, iron working might have spread more slowly in the Aegean. Iron was known before the collapse, so this is a delay, not a world without iron.

sources.cite: Anthony Snodgrass, The Dark Age of Greece (1971)

views.name: Eric Cline
views.claim: Drought, earthquakes, raiders, revolts and broken trade fed each other until a connected system failed.
views.for: Everything fell within a few decades across a linked region.
views.against: A many-causes story is hard to test.

views.name: Robert Drews
views.claim: Raiders with javelins and swords learned to beat chariot armies.
views.for: Chariot warfare fades after the collapse.
views.against: Little direct evidence of a tactical revolution.

views.name: Langgut, Kaniewski and others
views.claim: A long drought starved the palace economies.
views.for: Pollen and sediment records; famine letters.
views.against: Dating of the cores is loose, and some regions show no drought.

unknowns: Who the 'Sea Peoples' were and how many came.
Whether the drought was regional or Mediterranean-wide.
Why Egypt and Assyria survived while the Hittites and Mycenaeans did not.

model.name: A Late Bronze palace state
model.note: Toy Turchin-style model, not fitted to any real state. A long cold-dry spell lowers what the land can carry; take it away and the toy's crisis comes about thirty years later. That is all it can say: it knows nothing of raiders, earthquakes or trade.
